answer.evidence: The hay load (rows 6-33) is drawn face-on. Its rounded dome (rows 6-9, widths 14-32) is only a silhouette taper. There is no back-to-front ellipse and no front-edge line with eave shadow. Horizontal straps at rows 15-16 and 24-25 run across the front face and do not mark a top. The wagon bed (rows 34-43) is a vertical plank face with a single lighter line at row 34. The wheels at the sides are flat profile strips with no top. Nothing shows a horizontal surface seen from above, so this reads as a front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate hay wagon is a prop of the same kind as the references. Measured facts: 7 visible tones per 16x16 tile, 0% near-flat coverage, and only 2% neutral dark edge pixels, so the outline is tinted, a dark brown beside the wood and hay. That matches the hedge (9 tones) and is well below the stall (17) and well (20). By eye, the hay body has about 4 steps (pale highlight, yellow, orange, dark shadow) with some dotted grain and rope lines. The wood frame and wheels have fewer steps, about 3, and the wheels look fairly plain. The overall silhouette is chunky and readable but a bit simple next to the stall and well, which carry more clusters and per-material ramps. The piece has no flat fills and no sticker outline, but the shading depth and detail are somewhat below the better references, and when in doubt it fails.

answer.evidence: The hay heap (rows 6-33) is a face-on mound. Its silhouette widens 14, 22, 32 over rows 6-8, but this is a dome with no front-edge line or eave shadow, and it is not an ellipse. The two horizontal bands at rows 15 and 24 are straps on the front face, not edges of a top surface. The wagon bed below (rows 34-43) is a plain front plank face with no top band or edge line, and the wheels are pure side profiles. No horizontal surface is visible anywhere on the main body, so it is a front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The outline is tinted: only 2% of dark edge pixels are neutral, and the lines read as dark brown beside the wood and dark ochre beside the hay, not black. The hay has speckle and rope lines, and the wood has plank lines, so there are no big flat fills (0% near-flat). The ramps are shallow, though. The hay has about 4 steps and the wood about 3, against roughly 6 per material on the stall and well. The whole piece uses only 12 distinct colours, with 7 visible tones per tile. The comparable large props, the cheese stall (17) and the roofed well (20), carry far more, and only the small hedge is close at 9. At this size the wagon body and wheels look flatter and simpler than those references, so a careful artist would not accept it beside them without more shading. When in doubt, fail.
